prompt.problem_text: Glass cutting: rectangular items of an order book are cut out of a sequence of identical large plates (6000 x 3210 mm, used in their given order) by guillotine cuts in three stages plus trimming: vertical 1-cuts through the whole plate (two consecutive 1-cuts are at least 100 and at most 3500 apart, waste and the final leftover excepted), horizontal 2-cuts through a strip (at least 100 apart, waste excepted), vertical 3-cuts, and at most one 4-cut in a piece obtained by a 3-cut (it separates an item from waste or two items); every piece of waste is at least 20 x 20. Items may be rotated by 90 degrees. The items come in STACKS: the items of a stack must be cut in the order of the stack (stacks are independent of each other). Every plate carries small DEFECTS (rectangles); no item may contain a defect and no cut may run through one. The COST is the waste: the area of the plates used - the last plate only up to its last 1-cut, what lies to the right of it is a reusable leftover - minus the area of the items (an integer, mm x mm; lower is better). An instance is three csv files: `<prefix>_batch.csv` (ITEM_ID;LENGTH_ITEM;WIDTH_ITEM;STACK;SEQUENCE), `<prefix>_defects.csv` (DEFECT_ID;PLATE_ID;X;Y;WIDTH;HEIGHT) and `global_param.csv` (plate size, number of plates, cut limits). A solution file is the csv of the cutting tree (PLATE_ID;NODE_ID;X;Y;WIDTH;HEIGHT;TYPE;CUT;PARENT; TYPE = item id, -1 waste, -2 branch, -3 leftover). The evaluation service passes every solution through the official checker of the problem (items, stack order, cut rules, defects) and recomputes the waste from it.
prompt.solver_text: a tree search that builds a cutting plan by inserting one item after another (the branching scheme: where the next item may go, which cuts that implies, how defects are avoided, symmetry and dominance rules) and explores the tree with a restarting best-first search of bounded memory guided by a criterion on partial plans; open-source C++ in `src/gc/` (`lib/` = instance and branching scheme, `ub_*/` = the search drivers); `src/params.txt` holds one line, the search that runs and its options (start: `MBA* c 1 f 1.5`); `src/host_main.cpp` is the program's interface, not part of the solver
prompt.time_text: 180 seconds for every order book, whatever its size
prompt.build_text: `g++ -std=gnu++14 -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG -w -pthread -I. host_main.cpp gc/lib/*.cpp gc/ub_*/*.cpp -o prog` in `src/` (new `.cpp` files must lie in `gc/lib/` or in a directory `gc/ub_<name>/`), after `params.txt` has been checked (ONE line: a search name known to `host_main.cpp` - MBA*, BS, BSS, A*, DFS, DPA* - followed by pairs `<letter> <number>`); a launcher `solver` is then written next to the binary; `python3 tools/problem.py build src bin` does exactly this in your directory
prompt.io_text: `solver <instance file> <solution file> -t <seconds> -seed <int>`: the launcher writes the csv files of the order book and starts the program as `prog <prefix> <seconds> <seed> <solution csv> "<line of params.txt>"`; the program must write the solution csv and print its one `RESULT ...` line as the original does
prompt.size_text: `--n` is the number of items (the service asks for sizes from {lo} to {hi}).

island_text:
This project is one of three that improve the same solver in parallel, all three on the same training instances. The MAIN project's solver is the one that will be tested at the end. Yours and one other are scouts: your role is to find ideas that neither of the other two projects has had. Your line of versions follows the main project: at the start of a session of yours the service may set your committed version to the main project's current one (announced in `NOTICES.md`; the work tree of your previous session is then kept in `before_sync/`), so that you work on the solver as it is now and not on an old one. Between two such moments your line is that version plus the changes you commit. How the three work together:
- Every change you commit is sent to the main project as an offer, with what it measured here; it decides by itself what to do with it (take it, build on it, or leave it). So: one change per commit, and a commit note that says what the change is and why it should make the solver better in general.
- `REF_*.md` are briefs of the two other projects (they appear once those projects have evaluated something, and are kept up to date): what each has kept, what it tried and did not keep, and what it is working on now. Nothing on them is for you to do: do not port or re-test what another project kept, do not retry what it dropped, do not duplicate what it is doing. Read the briefs before you choose an idea, and choose one that is on none of them. Your value is in the ideas that are different.
- Before you start on a new direction (before you write code for it), declare it: `python3 tools/ctl.py claim "<one sentence>"`. The answer gives the record of the other two projects: what each is working on now, what it declared earlier, what it kept, and what it tried and did not keep. If yours is the same idea as anything on that record, or a variant of it, do not start it: think of another and declare that one. One declaration at a time (a new one replaces the old one). The service refuses `probe` and `eval` until you have declared a direction, and again after every commit until you declare the next one.
island_note: its training instances are the same 10 families of order books as yours
